name: LM1875T_LF05
title: 20 W audio power amplifier, TO-220
summary: The LM1875 is a single-chip audio power amplifier in a five-lead TO-220. It gives 20 W into 4 Ω or 8 Ω from ±25 V and more than 30 W into 8 Ω from ±30 V, at 0.015 % THD (1 kHz, 20 W). It is compensated on chip for closed-loop gains of 10 and up, and has current limiting with safe-area reduction, thermal shutdown and output clamp diodes. Supply range is 16 V to 60 V, split or single.

circuits.title: Typical application, split supply
circuits.description: Non-inverting speaker amplifier on plus and minus rails. The input is AC coupled through C1; R1 holds the source side at ground and R2 sets the DC level of +IN. R4 from the output and R3 with C2 to ground set the closed-loop gain, C2 taking the gain to unity at DC. R5 and C5 load the output at high frequency. Each rail has a 0.1 µF ceramic and a 100 µF electrolytic to ground.

circuits.title: Typical application, single supply
circuits.description: Non-inverting speaker amplifier on one positive rail with -VEE at ground. R1 and R2 split the supply to a mid-rail bias that C2 filters, and R3 carries that bias to +IN. The signal enters through C1, with R4 to ground on the source side. R6 from the output and R5 with C3 to ground set the AC gain. The speaker is coupled through C6, 2200 µF, so it carries no DC; R7 and C5 load the output at high frequency. VCC is bypassed by 0.1 µF and 100 µF.

operation.text: Stable at closed-loop gains of 10 or more. Oscillation, where it appears, comes from board layout or from coupling between output and input. Load ground, output-network ground and the small-signal ground (input and feedback) each run on their own path back to the board's ground point; shared ground conductors carrying load current put signal voltages at the input. The output R-C network and the 0.1 µF supply bypass caps sit as close to the LM1875 as possible, with short ground returns.

Output lead current radiating back to the input can cause high-frequency oscillation, most often with a high source impedance or long input leads. A 50 pF to 500 pF capacitor across the input cures it.

A capacitor straight on the output with no series resistance makes the square-wave response ring above about 0.1 µF. Up to about 2 µF typically does not oscillate, though this is not recommended. For highly capacitive loads put at least 1 Ω in series with the output. A 5 µH inductor shunted by 10 Ω, placed between output and load, is a usual guard against low load impedance at high frequency.

Supply traces and wires are kept apart from input traces and wires, so the large non-linear supply currents do not couple inductively into the inputs. Supply wires are twisted together, kept off the board, and leave the board at right angles for a couple of inches. Laid out this way, THD into 8 Ω at 10 W is under 0.05 % at 20 kHz and under 0.02 % at 1 kHz.

operation.topic: Current limit and safe operating area
operation.text: Output current is limited to around 4 A, and the limit drops as the voltage across an output transistor rises, which protects the output stage when driving reactive loads.

Diodes from the output to each supply rail are built in. They catch a reactive load (a motor, or a speaker with protection relays) that tries to pull the output beyond the rails, so no external diodes are needed for ordinary reactive loads.

The die shuts down at 170 °C and restarts when it has cooled to about 145 °C. If it heats again, the next shutdown comes at 150 °C. A brief fault lets the die run hot; a lasting fault holds it to the lower temperature, which reduces thermal cycling stress. The heat sink is chosen so that shutdown is not reached in normal use.

A heat sink is always needed, even with no load. Idle current is up to 100 mA, so on 60 V the unloaded part dissipates 6 W; with the TO-220's 54 °C/W junction to ambient that would raise the die 324 °C above ambient, and thermal shutdown would act. Example: on a 50 V supply into 8 Ω the part can dissipate up to 19 W; for a die below 150 °C at up to 70 °C ambient the total junction to ambient must be under 4.2 °C/W. With θJC = 2 °C/W, interface plus sink must be under 2.2 °C/W. Case to sink is about 1 °C/W metal to metal lubricated, 1.2 °C/W dry, 1.6 °C/W with lubricated mica and 3.4 °C/W with dry mica. With lubricated mica the sink must be 0.6 °C/W. Limiting ambient to 50 °C (122 °F) relaxes this to a 1.6 °C/W sink; isolating the sink from the chassis and dropping the mica, with a lubricated interface, relaxes it to 1.2 °C/W.
On a single supply the tab is at ground potential, so the part can be bolted straight to the heat sink with no mica or other insulator, for the best heat transfer.

For a given impedance magnitude, more reactance means more dissipation in the amplifier. A 60° load, usually taken as the worst case for a loudspeaker, dissipates roughly what its real (resistive) part alone would. An 8 Ω, 60° speaker impedance has a 4 Ω real part, so dissipation follows the 4 Ω curve.
Built-in ESD protection is limited. Keep the leads shorted or the part in conductive foam while stored or handled, to protect the MOS gates.
